PHSCS 587

Schottky and ohmic contacts

From the figure to the concept

Fig. 1 shows how a thin barrier can allow a low-resistance contact despite band bending

Every device needs contacts, and a metal–semiconductor interface can either limit transport or serve as a nearly transparent connection. A Schottky barrier presents an energy barrier to a majority-carrier population. Its rectifying behavior depends on the barrier height, depletion width, applied bias and transport mechanism. Band bending is therefore part of the contact problem, even when the bulk semiconductor is neutral.

An ohmic contact has a sufficiently low, approximately linear voltage–current relation over its intended operating range. One route is a small effective majority-carrier barrier. Another is heavy contact-region doping that narrows the barrier enough for substantial tunneling. The contact can then be conductive even though a barrier remains in the band diagram.

The differential specific contact resistivity can be written ρc = dV/dJ near a stated bias, with units Ω·m². Actual contact resistance also depends on area and current spreading. Interface states, interfacial layers, processing and polarity matter. A generic metal choice or a work-function sketch alone does not establish a reliably ohmic fabricated contact.

Example

For a uniform ideal contact with the same ρc, doubling contact area halves its lumped differential resistance ρc/A. Real layouts can depart from this area scaling when current crowding limits the effective transfer area.

Practice

1. How can increasing semiconductor doping improve a contact without eliminating the barrier height?

Consider barrier width and transmission.

Higher doping can narrow the depleted barrier, making tunneling more probable and reducing contact resistance.
